q: What is the classic presentation of an extradural haematoma?
o: Loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then deterioration
why: Usually temporal, from the middle meningeal artery; the lucid interval is followed by rapid decline.

q: Which vessel is most commonly injured in an extradural haematoma?
why: A temporal bone fracture often tears the middle meningeal artery.

q: What PaCO2 target is used during surgery for an extradural haematoma?
why: Normocapnia (4.5–5 kPa); avoid hypoxia and hypotension, which worsen secondary brain injury.

q: Should surgery be delayed to place an arterial line in a deteriorating patient with an extradural haematoma?
o: No: do not delay surgery to place an arterial line
Yes, and a CVC as well
why: Time is critical; do not delay surgery or transfer for invasive lines.

q: How is the severity of TBI classified by GCS?
What CPP target is used in severe TBI (tier 1)?
why: Tier 1: head up 30°, deep sedation, PaCO2 4.5–5 kPa, PaO2 over 10 kPa, ICP monitoring, CPP 60–70 mmHg.

q: ICP remains above 22 mmHg despite tier 1 measures in TBI. What is a tier 2 option?
o: 20% mannitol 0.5 g/kg or hypertonic saline (target Na 150–155)
why: Tier 2 (after repeat CT): optimise PaCO2 to 4–4.5 kPa, mannitol or hypertonic saline. Tier 3: decompressive craniectomy or barbiturate coma.

q: Why should ETT ties be loose in a patient with raised ICP?
o: Tight ties impede jugular venous drainage and raise ICP
why: Avoid tight ties and keep the neck neutral to aid venous drainage.

q: What did the CRASH-3 trial show?
o: Tranexamic acid reduced head injury death in mild–moderate TBI when given early
why: CRASH-3 supported early TXA in isolated TBI, with benefit in mild–moderate injury.

q: Which effect of altitude matters during air transfer of a ventilated head-injured patient?
why: Gas expands at altitude: check cuff pressure and drain pneumothoraces; PaO2 falls.
